doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

chapter: Studio craft and the TV and rock dates
title: How to prioritize reading a new chart; studio writers' personalities
summary: Shew's order for scanning music (tempo, key, roadmap) and how he knew film and TV writers like Herrmann, Goldsmith and Peter Matz.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Hardly ever. Almost never. My wife could look at my face, the wrinkles in my face and tell whether I enjoyed myself or not. And she could tell. She said, “Another one, ey?” But I wanted to back up a little bit, Monk, if you don’t mind, just because there’s a thing about in the studio thing, it’s a very, you know I mean what I had to do, what I did was different than what you were talking about the student who sings the two measure phrase.

The first thing, there’s a way of prioritizing the way you look at a piece of music. You’re only going to see it one time, you’re never going to see it again ever in your life probably, ever. You know? If you’re lucky. And the thing about it is the first thing you want to look at is, and a lot of people will say, “Look at the key signature first. Second, look at the key signature.” But look at the first thing is the tempo. Find out how fast this thing is going to go first. Because if you look down and see five sharps you go oh my God. And then it says “largo” ahh I’m cool. You follow what I’m saying?

Like you have to know the right priorities in order to salvage yourself spiritually in a situation like that because you can psychologically turn yourself into a banana pie if you don’t watch out, real quick. So like you look at the tempo, then look at the key signature, then look at the roadmap. Where are the endings? Is there a coda? Where is the coda sign? Where does it go to? Where are the repeats? Like know the roadmap, where you’re going to get in, where you’ve got to go back to if at all. Then you start looking in at where you see a lot of tricky measures, where you see a lot of notes in a measure. Then, that — if you look at that first you don’t even know what tempo it’s got to be in. And you haven’t got the key signature sorted. And the priorities — at least in my opinion, were tempo, key signature, roadmap. That’s first and foremost. And then start looking at the notes and see if there’s anything that looks a little scary: high, lots of ledger lines, or lots of sixteenth notes in a measure, or a lot of funny kind of things. But if you prioritize it you save yourself an awful lot of stress by doing it that way you know. And the problems with being in a studio is when the contractor or the service, when the answering service calls you and books you on a studio and a time, sometimes they’ll tell you who the writer is and sometimes they don’t. If they say Bernard Herrmann, you go ohhhh shit. Take the Valium with me you know. Put a pint of whiskey in my horn case. Because Bernard Herrmann’s going to be a pain in the ass. He’s going to be — he’s like Hitler you know? Real militant and screaming and hollering and things like that. If it’s Jerry Goldsmith it’s going to be much more relaxed. If it’s Johnny Mandel it’s going to be different. And you get to where you know these people, these writers, and some of them, like Peter Matz who I did an awful lot of stuff with Peter Matz, he was Barbra Streisand’s conductor when I worked with her an awful lot. And Peter was like the writer on the “Carol Burnett Show” you know, the director and all that. I didn’t do the “Carol Burnett Show” but we did Tony Orlando and Dawn right across the hall from them, but I got to know Peter really well. And Peter’d come up and he’d hug you and everything, “Yeah, Bobby.” You know you could go up to some of the other ones and they didn’t even know your name even after you’d done a hundred sessions with them you know.
